title: Number of Provinces (Union-Find)
description: Count connected components in an n x n adjacency matrix using Union-Find with path compression. Each union of two distinct roots merges two components — start with n, subtract one per successful union.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I get an n×n adjacency matrix `isConnected` where `isConnected[i][j] === 1` means cities i and j are directly connected, and I need to count provinces — where a province is a group of cities mutually reachable (directly or transitively)."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Symmetric — the matrix is symmetric, right? `isConnected[i][j] === isConnected[j][i]` for all i, j? (Undirected friendships.)
• Diagonal — `isConnected[i][i] === 1` always (a city is always connected to itself)? Doesn't matter for the algorithm but worth confirming.
• Values — strictly 0 and 1, never anything else?
• `n=1` — single city, single province, return 1?
• `n=0` (empty matrix) — return 0?
sections.why: The symmetry confirmation matters because it's what lets us iterate only the upper triangle (`j > i`) and process each edge exactly once. If the matrix could be asymmetric (e.g., 'i follows j' rather than 'i is friends with j'), this becomes a directed-graph problem and Union-Find doesn't fit cleanly. The diagonal question is paranoia — `isConnected[i][i]=1` triggers `union(i, i)`, which is a no-op for Union-Find (same root) but worth noting. Asking signals you're paying attention to the data model, not just the algorithm.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious approach before optimizing.
sections.say:
"This is the same problem as Connected Components, just with a different input encoding — the matrix IS the adjacency structure. Two solutions, basically equivalent in complexity:

1. **DFS from each unvisited city.** Treat `isConnected[i]` as the neighbor list for city i (where j is a neighbor iff `isConnected[i][j] === 1`). Outer loop over cities; each unvisited launch is a new province. O(n²) — we scan the entire matrix to compute neighbors.

2. **Union-Find.** Walk the upper triangle; for each `isConnected[i][j] === 1` with `j > i`, union i and j. Count remaining distinct roots. Also O(n² · α(n)).

Brute force in the sense of 'pairwise reachability check' would be O(n³ + n⁴) — for each pair (i, j), BFS to see if reachable. Obviously dominated by either of the above. I'll go with Union-Find here because it pairs cleanly with the matrix-edge enumeration: every `[i][j]=1` IS an edge, and `union(i, j)` consumes it directly. Decrement a `count` from `n` on each successful merge — final count is the answer."
sections.why: Two reasons to name both algorithms. (1) It frames the choice — most candidates default to DFS for this problem because it's labeled 'graphs', but Union-Find is genuinely cleaner when the input is already an edge list (or in this case, an edge matrix). (2) The decrement-from-n trick is the specific implementation insight that distinguishes 'I know Union-Find' from 'I've actually used Union-Find for counting components' — most candidates initialize `count = 0` and try to derive it at the end, which requires either a second pass or a Set of roots.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to Union-Find?
sections.say:
"'Count groups in a fully-given undirected graph with edges already enumerated' is the connected-components signature, and the matrix format is the explicit tell for Union-Find: each `[i][j] = 1` IS a `union(i, j)` call. Read the matrix once, fire all the unions, count distinct roots — that's the entire algorithm.

The Union-Find structure: `parent[i] = i` initially (every city is its own province), with `find(x)` walking parents until it hits a fixpoint AND applying path compression on the way up (halving — `parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]` each step — keeps amortized find near O(α(n))). `union(a, b)` does `parent[find(a)] = find(b)`; only count it if the roots differ.

The counter trick: start `count = n`. On every successful union (different roots), `count--`. At the end, `count` IS the number of remaining components. No second pass through `parent` needed.

Why Union-Find and not DFS here? Both are O(n²) in this matrix encoding, but Union-Find is structurally cleaner: the iteration pattern (upper triangle of the matrix, union on every 1) is a direct translation of the input. DFS would require building or implicitly walking the adjacency, which is an extra mental step. For the streaming variant (cities become friends over time, report province count after each), Union-Find is the only game in town because DFS would have to re-scan from scratch."
sections.why: Naming the pattern AND the count-down trick AND the streaming-variant motivation is what makes this conversation feel earned. 'Use Union-Find' is the trigger; 'use Union-Find because the matrix is an edge list and the count-down-from-n trick makes the component count a side effect of the unions, not a separate computation' is the derivation. The streaming-variant call-out is the killer follow-up — interviewers love asking 'what if friendships were added one at a time?' and the answer is 'Union-Find handles it incrementally; DFS would need to re-run on every addition.'

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a 5-city case with two distinct provinces, all-isolated (no edges in the upper triangle), and fully-connected (every union merges).

examples.note: Two provinces — {0,1} via edge 0-1 and {2,3,4} via edges 2-3, 3-4. Confirms upper-triangle iteration covers each edge once.
examples.trace:
init: parent=[0,1,2,3,4], count=5
(i=0,j=1): [0][1]=1 → find(0)=0, find(1)=1, differ → parent[0]=1, count=4
(i=0,j=2..4): all 0 → skip
(i=1,j=2..4): all 0 → skip
(i=2,j=3): [2][3]=1 → find(2)=2, find(3)=3, differ → parent[2]=3, count=3
(i=2,j=4): [2][4]=0 → skip
(i=3,j=4): [3][4]=1 → find(3)=3, find(4)=4, differ → parent[3]=4, count=2
return 2

examples.note: Degenerate diagonal-only — no edges in the upper triangle, no unions, count stays at n.
Every pair is an edge; first union merges, subsequent unions hit same-root and are no-ops.
examples.trace:
init: parent=[0,1,2,3], count=4
(i=0,j=1): differ → parent[0]=1, count=3
(i=0,j=2): find(0)=1 (via path-compressed walk), find(2)=2, differ → parent[1]=2, count=2
(i=0,j=3): find(0)=2 (compressed), find(3)=3, differ → parent[2]=3, count=1
(i=1,j=2): find(1)=3, find(2)=3, SAME root → no-op, count stays 1
(i=1,j=3): find(1)=3, find(3)=3, SAME → no-op
(i=2,j=3): find(2)=3, find(3)=3, SAME → no-op
return 1

sections.why: Tracing surfaces the two things that the algorithm description hides. (1) The fully-connected case proves that the 'only decrement count on different roots' check matters — without it, you'd decrement 6 times (one per upper-triangle pair) and end up with `count = -2`. The same-root no-op is what keeps the count honest. (2) Watching the path compression in action — `find(0)` in the third union returns 2 directly because the previous walk re-pointed `parent[0]=1` and then `parent[1]=2` — shows why future finds get faster. On a real adversarial input this is the difference between O(n² log n) and O(n² · α(n)).

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• `n=0` (empty matrix) → outer loops don't execute, return count=n=0. ✓
• `n=1, isConnected=[[1]]` → loops don't execute (j starts at 1), count=1. ✓
• All-zeros adjacency matrix (impossible since diagonal is 1, but excluding the diagonal: `[[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]]`) → no unions, count=n=3. ✓
• Fully connected → one province, count=1. The same-root check prevents miscounting.
• Forgetting `j > i` and using `j = 0` instead → every edge is unioned twice (once as (i,j), once as (j,i)). Correctness-preserving (second call is same-root no-op) but doubles the work. The upper-triangle is a constant-factor optimization, not a correctness requirement.
• Forgetting path compression → unions can degenerate into a linked list; find becomes O(n) per call, total O(n³). Path compression is what makes the algorithm near-linear-per-union.
• Forgetting the `ra !== rb` check → every union decrements count, including no-op unions on same-root pairs. `count` ends up negative or wrong. The check is the single most important line.
• Non-symmetric matrix (asymmetric isConnected) — algorithm assumes symmetry. If `[0][1]=1` but `[1][0]=0`, the algorithm still unions 0 and 1 once (when iterating `i=0, j=1`) — but the input is malformed. Worth flagging."
sections.why: The 'ra !== rb' rule is the load-bearing line — bugs there silently give wrong answers, not crashes, which is the worst kind. The 'upper triangle vs full square is a constant factor, not correctness' insight is the subtle one that separates 'I memorized to do j=i+1' from 'I understand WHY j=i+1 is faster but not required' — interviewers love distinguishing those. Forgetting path compression is the other silent failure: still correct, just slow. Calling out the difference between correctness bugs and performance bugs is the senior move.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n² · α(n)) ≈ O(n²) for all practical inputs. The outer loops are O(n²) over the upper triangle. Each iteration does at most two `find` calls plus a possible parent update; with path compression, `find` is amortized O(α(n)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function — bounded by 4 for any conceivable input size. So effectively constant per find. Total: O(n²).

Space is O(n) — just the `parent` array. No adjacency list built; we read the matrix directly.

If you wanted to extend to Union by Rank (track the depth of each tree, attach the shallower to the deeper) on top of path compression, you'd get strict O(n² · α(n)) — same asymptotic but tighter constants. For this problem the path-halving compression alone is usually enough.

If you wanted to switch to DFS: build an adjacency list from the matrix (O(n²)), then `for i in 0..n-1: if !seen[i] then count++ and DFS(i)`. Same O(n²). DFS is what I'd reach for if the problem already gave me an adjacency list (Connected Components encoding); Union-Find is what I reach for when edges come as a matrix or stream.

The same template — 'each true entry in the matrix is a `union(i, j)` call; decrement count from n on each successful merge' — shows up in Friend Circles (literally this problem with different naming), Number of Islands II (streaming additions on a grid), Accounts Merge (union on shared emails), and Redundant Connection (union, and the first edge that fails-to-union is the redundant one)."
sections.why: The α(n) defense is the textbook Union-Find argument — interviewers may ask 'why is find amortized constant?' and the answer is 'path compression flattens the trees, so future walks are short; the worst-case is bounded by inverse Ackermann, which is at most 4 for n < 2^65536.' The Friend Circles cross-reference is the killer: it IS this problem with a different name and a different LeetCode number, so the same algorithm is literally a copy-paste. The Redundant Connection extension is the elegant one — 'first edge whose union fails is the one that closes the cycle' is a beautiful application of the same primitive.

walkthrough.intro: Step through Union-Find with path compression. Each city starts as its own province; every successful union of two distinct roots drops the count by one. Watch parent[] flatten as finds compress paths.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter findCircleNum — ${n}x${n} matrix`, state: { matrix: isConnected.map(r => [...r]), n } };
const parent = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => i);
yield { line: 4, label: `init parent=[${parent.join(',')}] — every city is its own root`, state: { parent: [...parent], n } };
yield { line: 12, label: `init count=${count} (n singleton sets)`, state: { parent: [...parent], count } };
for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
yield { line: 15, label: `scan (i=${i},j=${j}) — isConnected[${i}][${j}]=${isConnected[i][j]}`, state: { parent: [...parent], count, i, j } };
yield { line: 17, label: `edge ${i}-${j}: find(${i})=${ra}, find(${j})=${rb}`, state: { parent: [...parent], count, i, j, ra, rb } };
yield { line: 21, label: `union: parent[${ra}]=${rb}, count → ${count}`, state: { parent: [...parent], count, i, j } };
yield { line: 19, label: `same root (${ra}) — already merged, count unchanged`, state: { parent: [...parent], count } };
yield { line: 26, label: `return ${count}`, state: { parent: [...parent], count, returns: count } };

notes: The matrix is symmetric — only iterate j > i to avoid double-unions.
Decrement count only on a SUCCESSFUL union (different roots). Same root → already in one province.
Path compression (halving or full) keeps amortized union/find at near O(α(n)) — effectively constant.

questions.q: Why iterate j from i + 1 instead of 0?
options: The matrix is symmetric; (i,j) and (j,i) are the same edge
Performance hack with no correctness impact

questions.q: When do you decrement the province count?
options: Only when find(i) and find(j) return different roots
Guarantees rank-balanced merges between two roots
Flattens the tree so future finds run faster

questions.q: For the matrix [[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,1]] the answer is:
questions.explain: Rows 0 and 1 are connected; row 2 is alone — two provinces.
